samples.summary: Image `alt` is written into the exported `.md` with only `\` and `]` escaped, so an attacker-controlled alt breaks out of `![...]` and injects raw HTML/Markdown — the same delimiter breakout this change just closed for `href`/`src`
samples.evidence: `escapeMarkdownAlt` (markdown.ts:325-327) escapes only `[\\\]]`. It does NOT escape `<` (which `escapeMarkdownText` at :318 *does* escape for body text) and does not reject newlines, while the new `UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS` gate (:263) is applied only to the URL, never to `alt`. `imageInline` (:296, :308) then emits `![${alt}](...)` verbatim. Vector: an attacker supplies `image.alt = "pic\n\n"`. Alt is attacker-influenceable through exactly the ingress paths the diff's own comment cites — `packages/docs/src/view/clipboard.ts:117` copies `alt` straight out of pasted clipboard JSON with no validation, `packages/docs/src/view/editor.ts:3692` takes it from `insertImage({alt})`, and a collaborator can write it over the CRDT. The victim exports Markdown (`packages/frontend/src/app/docs/text-actions.ts` → `serializeMarkdown(doc, {inlineImages:true})`) and the downloaded file contains: ![pic ](https://ok/x.png) The blank line ends the paragraph, so the trailing `` lands as a raw-HTML block in the exported document and fires in any renderer that passes raw HTML through (local previews, static-site generators, `marked`/`markdown-it` with `html: true`). This is precisely the "validator never looks at the bytes we emit" class the change documents at :239-262, left unfixed one line below the fix.

samples.summary: The new `assertUsablePageSetup` guard is bypassed by DOCX import and by any `setDocument` write, so a hostile `.docx` still persists NaN/closed-box page geometry into the CRDT for every collaborator
samples.evidence:
`assertUsablePageSetup` (packages/docs/src/view/editor.ts:960-993) is called only from `writePageSetup` (editor.ts:2062). The comment there states the invariant exists because bad geometry "would be persisted into the CRDT for every collaborator" — but that is not the only write path.

Bypass: `parsePageSetup` (packages/docs/src/import/docx-parser.ts:300-314) takes `w:pgSz/@w:w`, `@w:h` and the four `w:pgMar` values from the uploaded file with `Math.round(twipsToPx(parseInt(v,10)))` and no bounds check at all — `w:w="abc"` yields `NaN`, `w:w="-1000"` yields a negative width, `w:left="9999999"` yields margins far wider than the page. `docx-importer.ts:137,158` returns that as `document.pageSetup`, and the importer's document is stored via `setDocument`, which writes `root.pageSetup` directly (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.ts:2872-2876 and :2898-2902) — never through `writePageSetup`. Remote CRDT sync (`readPageSetup`, yorkie-doc-store.ts:604) likewise applies whatever a peer wrote with no validation.

So an attacker who can get a victim to import a crafted `.docx` (or who has edit access to a shared doc) stores exactly the state the guard declares unlayoutable, and it is replicated to every collaborator on open — a persistent client-side denial of the document. The added guard covers only the two callers that already respected the rule, which makes the invariant read as enforced when it is not.

samples.summary: `escapeMarkdownText` neutralizes Markdown punctuation but not newlines, so a text run containing a blank line escapes its block and can forge document structure (and truncate a GFM table row)
samples.evidence: `escapeMarkdownText` (:317-319) escapes `[\\*_[\]`~<]` and nothing else. A run whose `text` contains `\n\n` — reachable from HTML paste / clipboard JSON / CRDT, none of which strip newlines from run text — ends the current block, so everything after it is emitted as an independent Markdown block (e.g. a forged `# Heading`, `---` rule, or a GFM bare-URL autolink that was never a link in the source document). In `cellToMarkdown` (:167-182) only `|` is escaped, so the same newline terminates the table and the remainder of the row's content escapes the table entirely. Lower impact than the alt case because `<` *is* escaped here, so raw HTML cannot be smuggled through this path — but it is the same emit-what-you-did-not-validate gap the change set out to close.

samples.summary: `data:` detection is case-sensitive while the new `SAFE_IMAGE_DATA_URI` allowlist is case-insensitive, so `DATA:image/png;base64,…` is emitted inline even with `inlineImages` off
samples.evidence: `imageInline` computes `const isDataUri = image.src.startsWith('data:')` (:297) — case-sensitive — while `SAFE_IMAGE_DATA_URI` (:280-281) carries the `/i` flag. A src spelled `DATA:image/png;base64,AAAA` therefore fails the `isDataUri && !opts.inlineImages` placeholder branch (:298), passes `isSafeImageSrc` (:284-290) via the case-insensitive regex, and is written into the output. The CLI's documented `--inline-images=false` contract (docs/design/cli.md:764: "`data:` URLs become `[image]`") is bypassed by nothing more than capitalisation. No XSS follows — the MIME allowlist still holds — but two halves of one gate disagreeing on case is the kind of drift that becomes a hole when the allowlist next changes.

samples.summary: The PDF exporter still validates the WHATWG-normalized href and writes the raw string into the link annotation — the same parser differential the Markdown gate was just hardened against, left unhardened
samples.evidence: pdf-painter.ts:834 does `if (style.href && isSafeUrl(style.href)) addLinkAnnotation(page, rect, style.href)` — `isSafeUrl` judges what `new URL()` makes of the string (tabs/LF/CR deleted, leading/trailing C0-or-space trimmed) while the raw string is what reaches the PDF URI action. The new `isEmittableUrl` helper in markdown.ts:269 exists specifically to close that gap and was not applied here. I could not construct an escalation (I could not find a string that normalizes to an `http(s)`/`mailto` scheme yet reads as `javascript:` to a PDF viewer — embedded NUL/newline at worst truncates or mangles the target), so this is reported as unhardened-consistency rather than a demonstrated exploit; the fix is to route this call through the same emittability check.

samples.summary: `safeFilename`, now extended to the two new text exports, strips only `\/:*?"<>|` — control characters, bidi overrides and a leading dot survive into the download name
samples.evidence: export-utils.ts:110 sanitizes with `/[\\/:*?"<>|]+/g`. A document title containing `\r\n`, `‮` (RLO, used to disguise an extension as `…fdp.txt` → `txt.pdf`) or a leading `.` passes through into `a.download` (downloadBlob, :61-71). Path separators are stripped so traversal is not reachable, and browsers do their own final sanitisation of `download`, which is why this is a nit rather than a finding with teeth. Pre-existing and identical for the already-shipped `.pdf`/`.docx`; the change only widens the `ext` union, and docs/tasks/active/20260829-docs-surface-existing-features-todo.md already records it as a known limitation. Noted so it is not lost.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo. `escapeMarkdownAlt` (packages/docs/src/serialize/markdown.ts:325-327) escapes only `\` and `]`; it does not escape `<` even though `escapeMarkdownText` (:317-319) does for body text, and the `UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS` gate (:263, applied at :270 and :288) that rejects whitespace/C0-C1 controls is applied only to href/src, never to alt. `imageInline` (:296, :308) then interpolates the alt verbatim into `![alt](src)`. Ingress is unvalidated: clipboard.ts:110-118 assigns `image.alt` from pasted JSON via `asString` (clipboard.ts:65-67), a bare typeof check with no content restriction, and model/types.ts:133 declares `alt?: string` free-form so a CRDT collaborator can write it. The sink is reachable from packages/frontend/src/app/docs/text-actions.ts:44 (`serializeMarkdown(doc, {inlineImages: true})` for the downloaded .md) and packages/cli/src/docs/content.ts:129. An alt of "pic\n\n" therefore breaks out of the `![...]` segment and lands as a raw-HTML block in the exported file, executing in any renderer that passes raw HTML through. This is the same parser-differential/unsafe-output class documented at :239-262 and closed for URLs, left open for alt — in the security lane (injection / unsafe output handling), no guard elsewhere neutralizes it, code is exactly as the reviewer described.

finding.summary: The new `assertUsablePageSetup` guard is bypassed by DOCX import and by any `setDocument` write, so a hostile `.docx` still persists NaN/closed-box page geometry into the CRDT for every collaborator
finding.evidence:

So an attacker who can get a victim to import a crafted `.docx` (or who has edit access to a shared doc) stores exactly the state the guard declares unlayoutable, and it is replicated to every collaborator on open — a persistent client-side denial of the document. verdict.reason: Every element of the finding checks out against the repo. `assertUsablePageSetup` (packages/docs/src/view/editor.ts:962-993) has exactly one caller, `writePageSetup` (editor.ts:2062), whose comment claims the invariant protects CRDT-persisted geometry. `parsePageSetup` (packages/docs/src/import/docx-parser.ts:288-320) converts attacker-controlled `w:pgSz`/`w:pgMar` attributes with `Math.round(twipsToPx(parseInt(v,10)))` at lines 300-301 and 307-314 with no finiteness, sign, or margins-vs-page check, so `w:w="abc"` yields NaN and oversized margins yield a closed content box. That value is returned as `document.pageSetup` (docx-importer.ts:137,158) and reaches the CRDT through a fully reachable chain that never touches `writePageSetup`: upload-queue.ts:373 -> :379 applyContent -> apply-imported-content.ts:224 `new YorkieDocStore(doc).setDocument(...)` -> yorkie-doc-store.ts:2872-2878 and :2898-2903, which assign `root.pageSetup` directly. The remote-read side is unguarded too: readPageSetup (yorkie-doc-store.ts:530-543) only coerces with `Number(...)`, so NaN survives, and it is applied at :604 and :664. I found no compensating validation in docx-parser.ts, docx-importer.ts, apply-imported-content.ts, or setDocument. This is untrusted file-format input persisted into shared collaborative state, i.e. an added gate that reads as enforced while a bypassing write path exists — squarely the security lens's "weakest entry point" concern, and blocking at major.

finding.summary: Markdown URL gate validates a WHATWG-normalized URL but emits the raw string: an href/src containing a tab or newline passes `isSafeUrl` and breaks out of the link destination, injecting arbitrary Markdown/raw HTML into the exported `.md`.
finding.evidence: `isSafeUrl(href)` (packages/core/src/url/index.ts:26) parses with `new URL(...)`, and the WHATWG URL parser removes every ASCII tab/LF/CR from the input before parsing. The value written to the file is the untouched `style.href` — `escapeMarkdownHref` (markdown.ts:296) escapes only `\` and `)`, not whitespace or control characters. Chain: an attacker-controlled document run carries `href = "https://example.com/\n\n"`. Nothing validates href on the way into the model — HTML paste copies the attribute verbatim (packages/docs/src/view/clipboard.ts:597-599, where ` ` in a pasted `` decodes to a real newline), as do DOCX import and a collaborator writing the CRDT directly. `new URL` strips the newlines, sees `https:`, so line 224 accepts it; line 225 then writes the raw newlines into the file, producing: [click](https://example.com/ ) The link syntax is terminated by the newline and the remainder becomes a top-level block. Any renderer of the exported file that permits raw HTML (marked's default, markdown-it with `html:true`, a docs-site build pipeline) executes it. Line 270 (`![alt](${escapeMarkdownHref(image.src)})`) has the identical hole on the `isSafeUrl(src)` branch; the `data:` branch is safe because `SAFE_IMAGE_DATA_URI` (line 247) is anchored and excludes whitespace. Note the serializer already escapes `<` in text runs (line 280), so the file otherwise treats raw-HTML injection as in scope. Fix: emit `new URL(href).href` (the string that was actually validated), or reject any href containing whitespace/C0 control characters before writing.

verdict.reason: The code is not as described. The finding asserts markdown.ts line 224 gates with a bare `isSafeUrl(href)` and then emits the raw string, leaving the WHATWG tab/LF/CR normalization differential open. In this repository line 224 reads `if (style.href && isEmittableUrl(style.href))`, and `isEmittableUrl` (markdown.ts:269-271) is `!UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS.test(url) && isSafeUrl(url)` with `UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS = /[\s�--]/` (markdown.ts:263) tested against the RAW string before any parser touches it. `\s` covers tab/LF/CR/space plus Unicode spaces; the ranges cover C0/C1 controls. The finding's own payload `"https://example.com/\n\n"` is rejected there and the run degrades to plain text. The image path the finding calls "the identical hole" is closed the same way and earlier: `isSafeImageSrc` (markdown.ts:284-290) runs the character test FIRST, explicitly so it also covers the `data:image` branch that bypasses `isSafeUrl`, and `imageInline` returns `[image]` on failure (markdown.ts:305-307), so line 308 is unreachable with whitespace/controls in `src`. Grep confirms `escapeMarkdownHref` has exactly two call sites (225, 308), both behind the gate; there is no unguarded third emit path. The comment at markdown.ts:239-262 names this precise parser differential and justifies rejecting the characters over emitting `new URL(href).href`, and markdown.test.ts:557-564 has a dedicated "The parser differential" test section with BREAKOUT_PAYLOADS. `isSafeUrl` at packages/core/src/url/index.ts:24-31 is indeed a bare protocol check, but the serializer does not rely on it alone. The remediation the finding prescribes is already implemented in the stricter of the two forms it suggests.
